planting.note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Verrone's Obsidian pairs deep, near-black bronze foliage with small, single, deep red flowers, grown as much for its dramatic dark leaves as for its blooms.

directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where the darkest foliage color develops with the most direct light. Verrone's Obsidian belongs to the group of dark-foliage dahlias grown as much for their near-black, deeply bronzed leaves as for their flowers, and its small, single, deep red blooms with a contrasting yellow center provide a bright accent against the almost black foliage rather than dominating the plant. The bold, dark leaf color makes it a striking accent or backdrop plant in a mixed border, especially paired with silver or chartreuse foliage companions for contrast. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the compact plant blooming through summer, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store the tubers indoors after the first hard frost blackens the top growth.

common_name: Olivia Rose Austin (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall in soil enriched with compost; Olivia Rose Austin was named for the breeder's granddaughter and combines strong disease resistance with an exceptionally long repeat-flowering season.

directions: Set plants in full sun with at least six hours of direct light and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply and regularly during the first year to establish a strong root system. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to keep flushes of bloom coming. Olivia Rose Austin was bred by David Austin and named for his granddaughter, and it has become one of the most widely planted English roses for combining soft, cupped, blush-pink double blooms with a fruity fragrance and notably strong disease resistance compared to many older English rose cultivars, holding clean foliage through humid summers better than most. Its compact, bushy, well-branched habit makes it useful for smaller borders and mixed plantings where a full-sized shrub rose would be too large, and it repeats reliably from late spring through frost with regular deadheading.

common_name: Boscobel Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall in soil enriched with compost; Boscobel is a David Austin English rose bred for strong disease resistance and free-flowering habit, with salmon-pink blooms held upright on sturdy, twiggy stems.

directions: Set plants in full sun with at least six hours of direct light and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply and regularly during the establishment year. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season for continued bloom. Boscobel is one of David Austin's more disease-resistant English rose introductions, bred to hold clean, healthy foliage with minimal spraying even through humid summers, an advantage for Gulf Coast gardens where black spot pressure is heavy. Its rosette-shaped, salmon-pink to peachy-apricot double flowers with a light myrrh fragrance are held upright on strong, slightly arching stems, giving the shrub a neat, well-mannered look in the border rather than the floppy habit of some older English roses. It repeats reliably through the growing season with regular deadheading and moderate feeding.

common_name: The Generous Gardener Rose (David Austin Climbing English Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall in soil enriched with compost near a support structure; The Generous Gardener can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber, with fragrant, soft pink blooms and better shade tolerance than most roses.

directions: Set plants in full sun to light partial shade with rich, well-drained soil, and provide a trellis, fence, or pergola if training it as a climber, since it flowers well trained flat against a support or left as a large, arching, informal shrub. Prune to shape in late winter, removing only crossing or damaged canes if grown as a climber, and deadhead through the season to encourage repeat bloom. The Generous Gardener is a David Austin rose valued for its large, cupped, soft blush-pink double flowers with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance carrying notes of musk and myrrh, produced in generous flushes from late spring into fall. It tolerates a bit more shade than most roses, making it a useful choice for a partly shaded fence or wall where a typical rose would bloom poorly, and its long, flexible canes make it easy to train horizontally to maximize flowering along a support.
